hints: Focus on what makes these three forms similar, each carbon is sp2 bonded to three others with a spare p electron.
Compare flat sheets with a closed ball, graphene and graphite are flat hexagons but $\text{C}_{60}$ must curve using pentagons.
Think giant versus small, decide which allotrope exists as separate $\text{C}_{60}$ molecules rather than an endless lattice.
walkthrough:
**Check statement 1 for delocalised electrons**

All three allotropes use sp2 carbon. Each carbon forms three sigma bonds and leaves one p electron to join a delocalised pi system.

This is why graphene, graphite and $\text{C}_{60}$ all conduct electricity and show delocalisation:
$$\text{C (sp}^2\text{) : 3 sigma bonds + 1 delocalised p electron}$$

**Check statement 2 for 120 degree angles**

Graphene and graphite are flat layers of perfect hexagons, so the angle is the ideal trigonal planar $120^{\circ}$.

$\text{C}_{60}$ is curved into a ball with 12 pentagons and 20 hexagons, so the bonds are bent and the angles are pulled away from $120^{\circ}$.

**Check statement 3 for giant lattice**

Graphite (stacked layers) and graphene (single extended sheet) are giant covalent structures with endless C-C bonding.

$\text{C}_{60}$ is different. It is a simple molecular fullerene made of discrete $\text{C}_{60}$ molecules held by weak van der Waals forces, not a giant lattice. So only statement 1 is true for all three.

options.A: Incorrect. This implies statements 1, 2 and 3 are all correct for all three. Statement 1 is correct, but 2 fails for $\text{C}_{60}$ due to curvature and pentagons, and 3 fails because $\text{C}_{60}$ is simple molecular, not giant.
options.B: Incorrect. This implies statements 1 and 2 are correct. While delocalisation is common to all three, all bond angles are not $120^{\circ}$ in $\text{C}_{60}$ because the cage must close with five-membered rings and curved bonds.
options.C: Incorrect. This implies statements 2 and 3 are correct. Both are false for $\text{C}_{60}$. Its angles deviate from $120^{\circ}$ and it exists as separate molecules, so it cannot be described as a giant molecular crystalline lattice like graphite.
options.D: Correct. Only statement 1 applies to all three. Graphene, graphite and $\text{C}_{60}$ all have sp2 carbons with delocalised pi electrons, but only the flat forms have perfect $120^{\circ}$ angles and giant lattices.
